evidence: The LSM substrate is polycrystalline exhibiting several very sharp diffraction peaks which, as expected, loose intensity when the YSZ film thickness increases. In contrast, the intensity of the lines corresponding to the YSZ, increases with the film thickness. No shift is observed for either LSM or YSZ lines regardless of the film thickness. The three samples show well-crystallized phases already as-deposited without any annealing treatment. This is quite remarkable, since often ALD-deposited films are only slightly crystalline, due to the low deposition temperature. The average crystallite sizes of the substrate and YSZ layer were 38 and 18 nm, respectively. These values were calculated with the Scherrer formula from the full width at half maximum (FWHM) value of the strongest peak. The YSZ lines, for both cubic and tetragonal structures, extracted from JCDPS database, are listed in Table 1. It can be deduced that the layers processed by ALD show lines that can be ascribed to either cubic or tetragonal YSZ structure. The difficulty in distinguishing the cubic and the tetragonal phases is well-known and has already been addressed in a previous paper dealing with the deposition of YSZ onto LSM or other substrates by Bernay et al.. These authors mentioned that although the XRD lines for cubic and tetragonal phases are very close, the tetragonal structure can be corroborated because some of its characteristic lines may be split into two when the lattice parameters a and c do not match with c ¼ a √p. When the splitting does not occur, distinguishing the phases is impossible and other techniques are necessary, i.e. the Raman spectroscopy, which allows to explore the structural change between the cubic and tetragonal phases. Thus, the authors saw evidence by Raman spectroscopy for the presence of the YSZ cubic structure on porous LSM and for a mixture of cubic and tetragonal structures on porous Ni/YSZ (the usual SOFC anode). Therefore, we can conclude that in our case the YSZ cubic structure is dominant.
